<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the file tree and the README, this project is a Golang-based backend for a WhatsApp Multi Device API with both REST and WebSocket interfaces. It is designed as an API server that provides endpoints to manage WhatsApp sessions, send various types of messages, handle groups, users, newsletters, and more. Additionally, it contains front-end components (views and static assets) for user interactions as well as Docker and CI/CD configurations for building and deploying releases.

To create the best and most accurate system design diagram for this project, follow these detailed steps tailored to its specific architecture and purpose:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • API Server – This is the centralized core of the system, handling incoming HTTP requests and WebSocket connections.
   • REST API Layer – Located under src/internal/rest, this layer exposes endpoints (e.g., /app/*, /user/*, /send/*, /group/*, /message/*) which interact with the business logic.
   • WebSocket Handler – Under src/internal/websocket, this component manages persistent connections for real-time messaging.
   • Domain/Business Logic – Under src/domains and src/services, you have the business rules for each functional area (app, user, message, group, newsletter, send). This separation indicates a domain-driven design, where the “domains” package holds core models and the “services” package orchestrates use cases.
   • Utility and Library Layer – The src/pkg folder encompasses common utility functions, error handling (error types for app, validation, WhatsApp-specific errors), and WhatsApp client initialization/wrappers.
   • Configuration – The src/config and environment files (.env.example) support multi-layered configuration through command-line flags, environment variables, and .env files.
   • Frontend/UI – The src/views directory contains HTML and JavaScript (React-like components) for rendering the user interface (login, send messages, group management, etc.).
   • Documentation & API Specification – The docs folder, especially docs/openapi.yaml, details the API schema for client generation and integration.
   • Deployment – Docker-related files (docker-compose.yml, docker files, GitHub workflows) indicate that the system is containerized and built via CI/CD pipelines.

2. Outline the Relationships and Interactions:
   • External Clients (Web browsers, mobile apps, API consumers) interact with the API server via REST endpoints and WebSockets.
   • REST Controllers (located in src/internal/rest) call the corresponding Service functions (src/services) which in turn leverage Domain Models (src/domains) and Utility packages (src/pkg).
   • The authentication process, basic auth middleware and environment configuration ensure secure, configurable endpoints.
   • The UI (src/views) serves static assets for a web-based interface to interact with the API.
   • CI/CD and containerization components (GitHub workflows and Docker files) facilitate automated building, testing, and deployment.

3. Highlight Key Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Layered Architecture: The project shows a clear separation of concerns (API layer → Service layer → Domain models & utilities). This improves maintainability and scalability.
   • Domain-Driven Design: The “domains” folder indicates the encapsulation of business logic in discrete, functionally organized modules.
   • Configuration Priority: There’s a defined priority for configuration using command-line flags, environment variables, and .env files.
   • Containerization: Use of Docker and docker-compose along with CI/CD workflows shows an emphasis on reproducible builds and deployments.
   • RESTful & Event-driven Communication: With defined REST endpoints and a WebSocket component, the system uses both synchronous and real-time communication.

4. Include Relevant Technologies, Frameworks, and Libraries:
   • Golang as the core language.
   • Docker for containerization.
   • GitHub Actions for CI/CD.
   • ffmpeg (as an external dependency on supported OS) for media processing.
   • Swagger/OpenAPI (docs/openapi.yaml) for API specification.
   • Web technologies (HTML, JavaScript, and CSS) for the front-end.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • For this full-stack API server, clearly distinguish the backend components (REST API, business logic, configuration, and domain models) from the frontend static assets.
   • Emphasize integration points:
       - Show REST endpoints communicating with the service layer.
       - Illustrate WebSocket communication alongside REST.
       - Represent the flow from API invocation → service handling → domain logic and back.
   • Indicate deployment artifacts like Docker images and volumes used for persistent storage.
   • Highlight middleware components such as basic authentication and recovery in the REST layer.

6. Instruct the Engineer to Include the Following Diagram Elements:
   • Clear labels for each component:
       - “API Server”, “REST API”, “WebSocket Server”, “Business Services”, “Domain Models”, “Utility Libraries”, “Configuration Module”, “Frontend UI”, “External Clients”, “CI/CD Pipeline”, and “Containerization/Deployment”.
   • Directional arrows demonstrating communication flows (e.g., external client → REST API; REST API ↔ Service Layer; Service Layer → Domain Models; etc.).
   • Color coding or distinct shapes to differentiate between layers (for example, one color for API components, another for business logic, and another for external infrastructure like Docker/CI).
   • Annotations for configuration and deployment strategies (showing how command-line flags and environment variables influence behavior).

7. Additional Diagram Suggestions:
   • A layered or multi-tier diagram where:
       - The top level represents the Client/UI layer.
       - The middle level represents the API gateway – the REST endpoints and WebSocket handler.
       - The lower levels depict the domain/business layers and configuration/utility layers.
   • A separate inset or diagram section for “Deployment & CI/CD” illustrating how GitHub workflows and Docker integrate into the release process.

By following these detailed guidelines and ensuring every significant component (from request handling to business logic and deployment) is captured, the system design diagram will accurately reflect the project's structure and purpose. This explicit and component-focused design will be an excellent reference for understanding and maintaining the system. 
</explanation>
